newsitem.title: USA: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. worried by rapid rise in Japanese car imports.

text.p: U.S. trade officials expressed concern on Friday about rising Japanese car imports into the U.S. market and said Tokyo must do more to open Japan's markets to U.S. car products.

In an assessment of a hard-fought 1995 car trade agreement between the two countries, U.S. trade officials said progress has generally been positive. But they said they were disappointed in the slow pace of deregulation of Japan's car part market and in number of dealers who have agreed to sell U.S.-made cars in Japan.

"We are pleased that progress continues to be made under the agreement," U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley said in a statement. "U.S. vehicle sales in Japan jumped 34 percent and exports of U.S.-made automotive parts rose to $2 billion in 1996, an increase of 20 percent over 1995."

The 1995 agreement aimed at opening Japan's market to more U.S.-made cars and parts was signed in August 1995 after intense negotiations during which the two countries were on the brink of a tit-for-tat trade war.

The report by the Commerce Department and U.S. Trade Representative's Office to President Bill Clinton was more pessimistic than earlier assessments of the trade pact. It said Tokyo slowed the pace of deregulation of its parts market and that only 114 Japanese dealers signed up to sell U.S.-made cars, far short of the goal of 200 by the end of 1996.

U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said she was worried by trade trends that began to to develop in late 1996 and early 1997, particularly a surge in Japanese car imports in the U.S. market during the first three months of this year.

"We don't want to see a significant increase in the Japanese trade surplus," Barshefsky said. "The overall imbalance in U.S.-Japan auto trade and the first quarter surge in Japanese imports requires that we watch this situation closely."
A U.S. trade official told reporters that if Japan's trade surplus continues to rise significantly, tensions between the two countries were bound to increase as well.
"If the trend continues, we could see a renewal of trade frictions, and we want to avoid that, as do the Japanese," the official said in a telephone conference.

Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association General Director William Duncan said the report confirmed that Japan as met the requirements of the trade accord and any U.S. disappointments were due to unilateral expectations.

"It is alarming that the Clinton Administrtion would attempt to further distort the agreement by including within its scope references to auto imports into the United States which were not included in either the agreement or the discussions that led to it," he added.
The report said the weakening yen against the dollar benefited Japanese car makers at the expense of the Big Three U.S. manufacturers -- Chrysler Corp, Ford Motor Co and General Motors Corp.
Despite early gains in Japan after the trade agreement was signed, sales by the big three began to level off in late 1996 and declined in early 1997.

"In contrast, sales of European-made vehicles (including those produced by the Big Three) to Japan began to grow faster, in part because the yen did not depreciate as much against these currencies," the report said.

At the same time Japanese car makers took a bigger share of the U.S. market, the report said. U.S. car makers have complained for months that the weakening yen against the dollar was hurting their sales to Japan and giving Japanese car makers a competitive edge in U.S. markets.
Over the past two years, the Japanese yen has depreciated by more than 50 percent against the dollar, making Japanese goods cheaper and U.S. products more expensive.

"The weak yen is the single biggest threat to trade progress," American Automobile Manufacturers Association president Andrew Card said. "It threatens to nullify benefits of the 1995 auto pact." "It is the biggest obstacle to meaningful and measurable progress on bilateral auto trade."
Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto are scheduled to meet next Friday in Washington. U.S. officials have said trade concerns will be on the agenda.
